messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Fatima is an eighty-year-old widowed Palestinian-American woman who has spent the better part of five decades working as a social worker, accompanying other people through their worst moments with a steadiness she had always considered inseparable from who she was. That sense of herself — as someone capable, present, and useful in crisis — was profoundly disrupted eighteen months ago when her youngest son, Tariq, was admitted to the intensive care unit following a sudden and catastrophic cardiac event. He was forty-six years old. For eleven days, Fatima sat beside him in a room that hummed with monitors and smelled of antiseptic so sharp it seemed to coat the inside of her throat. She watched nurses thread IV lines into his arms, adjust drips, and replace bags of fluid with a clinical efficiency that she found both necessary and unbearable. She held his hand when he was conscious and stared at the ceiling when he was not, trying to find somewhere inside herself the composure she had offered to grieving families for decades. She could not find it. She remembers — though the memory arrives more often as sensation than image — the particular quality of helplessness she felt when a physician spoke to her in the corridor and she understood, for a few hours, that Tariq might not survive. Tariq did survive, but Fatima has not returned to the person she was before those eleven days.

In the weeks that followed his discharge, she began noticing that certain things undid her without warning. Driving past a hospital, catching sight of an ambulance, or glimpsing a needle on a medical television programme would produce a wave of distress so immediate it felt less like remembering and more like being returned. More disorienting still were the moments when the emotional weight of those eleven days arrived with no image attached — a sudden crush of grief and dread while she was washing dishes, with nothing she could point to as the cause. She has tried, with considerable effort, to push these moments away, to redirect her thoughts the way she might redirect a distressed client, but the memories do not respond to that kind of management. They arrive when they choose to.

What frightened Fatima most, as the months passed, was not any single symptom but the conclusion she was drawing from all of them together. She had come to believe that she was permanently altered — that the woman who had sat with bereaved parents and traumatised children and had remained, if not unmoved, then at least functional, was simply gone. She felt certain she had failed Tariq during those eleven days, that she had been passive and silent when she should have advocated more forcefully, and that this failure was a betrayal of values she had organised her life around. She also carried a quieter, more frightening conviction: that she could not protect the people she loved, that bad things would continue to find her, and that there was nothing she could do to prevent them.

These beliefs have shaped her days in ways that have accumulated into significant loss. Fatima, who once made home visits and attended community meetings and sat with families in hospitals without a second thought, has largely stopped going out. She declined a referral that would have required her to visit a client in a rehabilitation facility, citing administrative reasons, and her supervisor has gently noted her reduced caseload. She no longer attends the grief support group she once co-facilitated — conversations about people losing loved ones now feel less like professional territory and more like direct threat. A colleague who lost a parent recently mentioned it in passing, and Fatima excused herself from the room. Her social world, already quieted by widowhood, has contracted further.

It was her daughter who finally persuaded her to seek help, after Fatima cancelled a medical check-up for the third consecutive time and admitted, haltingly, that she could not make herself walk through those doors. Fatima came to the first session composed and precise, describing her symptoms in the careful language of someone who has spent a career naming other people's distress. What she is most afraid of, she said, is that she has used up whatever it was that made her good at her work. What she is hoping for, more quietly, is that she might be wrong about that.
